question_text: A company builds a regression model to predict house prices. The model needs to be evaluated on how well it predicts prices and the team wants a metric that is expressed in the same unit as the target variable (dollars) and that penalizes large prediction errors more heavily than small ones. Which metric should the ML engineer use?
explanation: RMSE (Root Mean Square Error) is expressed in the same units as the target variable (dollars) and penalizes large errors more heavily because it squares the errors before averaging. This makes it sensitive to outliers which is useful when large price prediction errors are especially costly. MAE (Mean Absolute Error) is also in the same unit but treats all errors equally rather than penalizing large errors more. R-squared is dimensionless (0 to 1) not in dollars. MAPE is a percentage not in dollars.
option_text: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)

question_text: A medical imaging model classifies X-rays as showing signs of tuberculosis or not. Missing a tuberculosis case (false negative) is far more dangerous than incorrectly flagging a healthy patient (false positive). Which metric should the ML engineer optimize to minimize the number of missed tuberculosis cases?
explanation: Recall (also called Sensitivity or True Positive Rate) measures the proportion of actual positive cases (tuberculosis) that the model correctly identifies. Maximizing recall minimizes false negatives — missed tuberculosis cases. Precision measures how many predicted positives are actually positive — it focuses on false positives not false negatives. Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets and does not specifically target false negatives. F1 Score balances precision and recall but does not specifically prioritize minimizing false negatives.
option_text: Precision

question_text: A fraud detection model is trained on a dataset where 99% of transactions are legitimate and 1% are fraudulent. The model predicts every transaction as legitimate and achieves 99% accuracy. What is wrong with using accuracy as the evaluation metric and which metric is more appropriate?
explanation: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets because a naive model that predicts the majority class for every example achieves high accuracy without learning anything useful. In this case predicting legitimate for every transaction achieves 99% accuracy while detecting zero fraud. F1 Score combines precision and recall and is specifically designed for imbalanced classification — it punishes models that ignore the minority class. AUC-ROC is also a good choice. Precision alone focuses on false positives not the complete picture. RMSE is a regression metric.
option_text: Accuracy is appropriate — 99% is an excellent result

question_text: A new version of a SageMaker recommendation model is ready for testing. The team wants to validate the new model against real production traffic without any risk of exposing users to potentially worse recommendations. The new model's output should be logged and compared to the production model but users should only receive recommendations from the current production model. Which deployment strategy should the ML engineer use?
explanation: Shadow testing (also called shadow mode deployment) is correct because it mirrors all production traffic to the new model in parallel but only serves users the production model's responses. The new model's outputs are logged for offline comparison. This provides validation against real traffic with zero user impact. A/B testing (production variants) exposes real users to both models which creates risk if the new model performs worse. Blue/Green deployment switches all traffic to the new model at once. Canary deployment gradually shifts real user traffic to the new model.
option_text: A/B testing with a 50/50 traffic split between old and new models

question_text: An ML engineer trains two models on the same dataset. Model A achieves AUC-ROC of 0.91. Model B achieves AUC-ROC of 0.79. The team plans to deploy the model at a very high precision threshold (0.95) to minimize false alarms. Which statement is correct about using AUC-ROC for this decision?
explanation: AUC-ROC measures overall model performance across all thresholds. When deploying at a specific operating point (high precision threshold) the relevant comparison is the Precision-Recall curve at that specific threshold not the overall AUC-ROC. A model with lower AUC-ROC could outperform a higher AUC-ROC model at a specific high-precision operating point. The team should compare the models specifically at the 0.95 precision threshold using the Precision-Recall curve. AUC-ROC alone does not answer which model is better at a specific operating threshold.
option_text: Model A is definitively better because 0.91 AUC-ROC is significantly higher than 0.79

question_text: A SageMaker training job runs for 6 hours. CloudWatch metrics show that training loss decreases continuously but at each epoch the validation loss is nearly identical to the training loss. Both losses are higher than the team's target. What does this pattern indicate and what should the ML engineer do?
explanation: When both training and validation loss are high and similar the model is underfitting — it lacks the capacity to learn the underlying patterns. The similar values for training and validation loss indicate there is no generalization gap, ruling out overfitting. The solution is to increase model capacity (more layers/neurons), reduce regularization strength if any is applied, or train for more epochs. Adding more dropout would further reduce capacity making underfitting worse. Reducing the number of features makes the problem harder for an already underfitting model.
option_text: Overfitting — add dropout regularization and collect more training data

question_text: A SageMaker training job for a deep neural network is monitored using SageMaker Debugger. The tool fires a built-in rule reporting that the loss tensor is NaN (not a number) starting from epoch 3. What is the most likely cause and the standard remedy?

question_text: A company builds a content moderation model to classify social media posts as policy violations or compliant. The test set contains 95000 compliant posts and 5000 policy violations. The model achieves 97.2% accuracy but the policy team says it is missing too many real violations. A confusion matrix reveals: TP=1500, TN=94700, FP=300, FN=3500. What is the recall and what does it indicate?
explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 1500 / (1500 + 3500) = 1500 / 5000 = 0.30 or 30%. The model is only catching 30% of actual policy violations — 70% of real violations are being missed (3500 false negatives out of 5000 actual violations). The high accuracy of 97.2% is misleading because the model is good at identifying the majority class (compliant) but poor at detecting the minority class (violations). The policy team is right to be concerned. This is the classic accuracy paradox on imbalanced datasets.
option_text: Recall = 97.2% — the model performs well and the policy team's concern is unfounded

question_text: An ML team builds a sentiment analysis model achieving 89% test accuracy. They release it and notice the model consistently misclassifies mixed-sentiment reviews containing both positive and negative phrases. SageMaker Debugger shows no gradient issues during training. The confusion matrix shows high true negatives and true positives but many mixed reviews (labeled neutral) are classified as either positive or negative. What is the most likely root cause?
explanation: The model was trained predominantly on clearly positive and clearly negative reviews with few neutral mixed-sentiment examples. The model learned to strongly classify one way or the other but never learned the nuanced mixed sentiment pattern. This is a training data distribution problem — the model cannot generalize to a category underrepresented in training. The solution is to collect more labeled examples of mixed-sentiment reviews and retrain. This is not an overfitting problem (which would show training-validation gap). Debugger shows no gradient issues so architecture is not the problem.
option_text: The model is overfitting — apply stronger L2 regularization and add dropout layers

question_text: A team trains a neural network on patient clinical data to predict readmission risk. The network has 12 hidden layers and 50 million parameters trained on 8000 patient records. The validation loss starts increasing significantly after epoch 5 while training loss continues decreasing steadily. SageMaker Debugger reports no gradient issues. What is the most accurate description of what is happening and what should be done?
explanation: This is textbook overfitting — the model (50M parameters) has far more capacity than the training data (8000 records) can support. The model memorizes training patterns including noise at the expense of generalizable features. The growing gap between training and validation loss confirms this. With 12 layers and 50M parameters for only 8000 records the model is massively overparameterized. Solutions include: reduce model size significantly, add strong dropout and L2 regularization, collect more training data, and implement early stopping at epoch 5.
option_text: Underfitting — 50 million parameters are insufficient for complex patient data

question_text: An ML team is comparing two binary classifiers for a clinical trial enrollment model. The team reviews the ROC curves for both models. Model A has AUC-ROC = 0.87 but at the operating point the team will use (very high recall threshold to catch all eligible patients) Model A's precision drops to 0.21. Model B has AUC-ROC = 0.81 but at the same operating threshold Model B's precision is 0.48. For the specific clinical use case which model is actually better?
explanation: AUC-ROC measures overall performance across all thresholds but the team has a specific operating requirement — very high recall for catching all eligible patients. At that specific threshold Model B delivers precision of 0.48 versus Model A's 0.21. At the operating point the team will actually use Model B performs better. This illustrates that AUC-ROC is a summary metric — at a specific operating threshold the Precision-Recall curve at that threshold is the definitive comparison. Higher overall AUC-ROC does not guarantee better performance at a specific operating point.
option_text: Model A because AUC-ROC of 0.87 is definitively better than 0.81

question_text: A company operates two SageMaker endpoints serving the same recommendation task. Endpoint A is the current production model. Endpoint B is a new candidate model. The ML engineer configures SageMaker production variants with 95% traffic to Endpoint A and 5% to Endpoint B. Business metrics show Endpoint B has 12% higher click-through rate over 2 weeks. The team now wants to gradually increase traffic to Endpoint B while maintaining the ability to immediately roll back to Endpoint A if metrics degrade. Which SageMaker deployment feature enables this?
explanation: SageMaker production variants allow dynamic traffic weight adjustment at any time without downtime. The team can gradually increase Endpoint B's weight from 5% to 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% while always maintaining the ability to immediately route all traffic back to Endpoint A by setting its weight to 100%. This provides the gradual rollout and instant rollback capability needed. Blue/Green deployment switches all traffic at once without a gradual ramp. Deploying a new endpoint loses the production variant traffic control. Shadow testing does not change which model serves real users.
option_text: Deploy a new dedicated SageMaker endpoint for Endpoint B and decommission Endpoint A when ready
